quote: Ferner ist auch noch die Frage, ob es Probleme in der Mathematik giebt, deren Erledigung [-eine immer gr-] nicht in einer vorge- schriebenen kleinen Zeit möglich ist? etc.
english: Furthermore there is also the question whether there are problems in mathematics whose settlement is not possible within a prescribed small time? etc.
topic: Hilbert reflects on the value of mathematical questions, distinguishing proofs that something is possible in finitely many steps from proofs giving an explicit upper bound, and asks whether some problems cannot be settled within a prescribed time; the page then begins a note about something he heard from Minkowski and Eberhard via others.

triage.modern_statement: Read in modern terms, the question asks whether there are well-posed mathematical decision problems that can be solved in principle (in finitely many steps) but cannot be solved within a prescribed bound on time or number of steps. In other words: is there a problem with no algorithm that runs within a given time bound f(n), or within some 'small' bound such as polynomial time? This is the basic question of computational complexity: lower bounds on running time and separations between time-bounded classes. Hilbert's wording ('vorgeschriebenen kleinen Zeit', 'etc.') is informal, so this reading is an interpretation and not an exact statement.
triage.answered_by: The general form was answered yes by J. Hartmanis and R. E. Stearns. Their time hierarchy theorem ('On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms', Trans. AMS 117, 1965) shows that for every suitable (time-constructible) bound some problems are decidable but not within that bound. A sharper version, whether natural problems can be solved in 'small' polynomial time, was raised by Gödel in his 1956 letter to von Neumann and became the P vs NP problem (Cook 1971 / Levin 1973). That version is still open. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, though it is related in spirit to the Entscheidungsproblem.

evidence.claim: The time hierarchy theorem, proved by Stearns and Hartmanis in 1965, shows that every deterministic time-bounded complexity class has a strictly larger time-bounded class, so some problems cannot be decided within a given time bound.
Hartmanis and Stearns, 'On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms', Transactions of the AMS 117 (May 1965).
Gödel's 1956 letter to von Neumann essentially described the P vs NP question about whether problems can be solved efficiently.
Gödel apparently saw the P vs NP problem as a finitary analogue of Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem.

triage.why: The page distinguishes three things: proving something is possible in finitely many steps, giving an explicit upper bound, and asking whether some problems cannot be settled within a prescribed time. This is clearly the distinction between computability and complexity. In its general form (problems that are decidable but need more than a given time bound), it was settled by the 1965 time hierarchy theorem. If 'small time' means efficient, i.e. polynomial, time for natural problems, the question becomes P vs NP and related lower-bound questions, which are open and actively researched.
